core_message: Since capturing Maduro, the US has shaped who governs Venezuela and who controls its oil, and the next test is an election promised for 2027.
title: What the US Is Doing in Venezuela, Mapped
description:
In January 2026, US forces captured Nicolás Maduro and flew him to New York. Ten months later, his former deputy runs the country with Washington's backing, a US-linked company holds 100-year rights to about a fifth of Venezuela's oil, and the opposition's Nobel laureate is back home asking when the election will be. Here is the map of America's role in Venezuela, step by step.

Facts as reported up to 1 November 2026, from Reuters, NPR, AP and others (sources below). Positions of each government are attributed to them.

Maps: country borders as shown by the Survey of India (Natural Earth, India view). Satellite imagery: NASA Blue Marble; contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2025-2026.

scenes.narration: On the third of January 2026, United States forces carried out a large military operation in Venezuela and captured its president, Nicolás Maduro.
scenes.heading: 3 January 2026

scenes.narration: Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, were flown to New York to face drug trafficking and weapons charges.
scenes.heading: Caracas to New York

scenes.narration: President Trump said the United States would run Venezuela until a safe transition.
Ten months on, who actually runs Venezuela? Who gets its oil? And when will Venezuelans get to vote?
Venezuela sits on the northern edge of South America, facing the Caribbean. Under it are the largest proven oil reserves of any country on Earth, about three hundred billion barrels.
scenes.heading: The world's biggest oil reserves

scenes.narration: Most of that oil is extra-heavy crude in the Orinoco Belt, a strip along the Orinoco River that is hard and expensive to produce.
scenes.heading: The Orinoco Belt

scenes.narration: Under Hugo Chávez and then Maduro, years of mismanagement and US sanctions cut production to a fraction of what it once was, and millions of Venezuelans left the country.
In July 2024, Venezuela's electoral council declared Maduro re-elected with about fifty-two percent of the vote.
scenes.heading: Caracas
scenes.text: Electoral council declares Maduro re-elected with about 52% of the vote
scenes.author: July 2024

scenes.narration: The opposition published its own tally from polling stations showing a clear win for its candidate, Edmundo González. Several governments and international organisations questioned the official result.
In 2025, the US built up warships in the Caribbean and began striking boats it said were carrying drugs.
scenes.heading: The Caribbean build-up

scenes.narration: Then came January, and the raid that took Maduro.
Venezuela's Supreme Tribunal ordered Vice-President Delcy Rodríguez to take over as acting president. The armed forces backed her.
She first called the US operation an illegal kidnapping. Within days she signalled that she was willing to work with Washington.
The US says it doesn't recognise her as democratically elected. But the Trump administration has backed her interim government, which was meant to last ninety days and is still in office.
In September, President Trump said it was too soon to consider elections.
And then there's the oil.
At the end of August, Trump announced an oil deal. Rodríguez's government granted a company called North American Blue Energy Partners hundred-year rights to seventeen oil fields.
scenes.heading: 17 fields, 100 years

scenes.narration: Those fields hold about sixty-five billion barrels of proven reserves, roughly a fifth of Venezuela's total.
scenes.heading: Barrels in the deal

scenes.narration: And the Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital will own thirty-five percent of the company.
scenes.heading: The Pentagon's stake

scenes.narration: The United States also gets the right to buy a fifth of the output at cost. The company has agreed to invest a hundred billion dollars, and the White House says the deal costs taxpayers nothing.
Many of those fields used to be run by Russian or Chinese companies.
scenes.text: Fields that were Russian and Chinese

scenes.narration: Critics in Washington object. Senator Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, called it a blatant abuse of power and taxpayer dollars. Analysts say reviving production will take years.
So the US now has a direct stake in Venezuelan oil, and in who governs the country that holds it.
scenes.text: A stake in oil and in power

scenes.narration: On the twenty-fifth of October, opposition leader María Corina Machado came home after about ten months abroad. She flew to Colombia and crossed into Venezuela by land.
scenes.heading: Machado comes home

scenes.narration: Machado had been barred from running in 2024. Last December she received the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway.
Crowds met her in Lara state and along an eight-hour drive to Caracas.
scenes.text: Crowds all the way to Caracas

scenes.narration: Secretary of State Marco Rubio called her return a direct result of US-supported reconciliation talks, which he said had freed hundreds of political prisoners. Her own movement was not part of those talks.
On the twenty-ninth, Machado said Rubio had laid out steps that make clear presidential elections will be held in 2027. She said Rodríguez also backed elections.
The talks are meant to overhaul the electoral council and the top court first.
So what to watch? Whether a date is set for the 2027 vote. Whether Machado's movement is let into the talks. And whether the oil deal survives the next government, in either country.
scenes.heading: What to watch
items: Does Machado's movement get a seat?

scenes.narration: For now, the country with the most oil in the world is run by an interim government that Washington backs, while its people wait for a vote.
scenes.heading: Waiting for a vote

scenes.narration: Should Venezuela hold its election sooner than 2027? Tell us in the comments.
